angle: PATENTS: Julius Blum GmbH (Hoechst, AT) patents and applications on radio links between a switch, remote, hub or sensor and an electric furniture flap drive (SERVO-DRIVE / AVENTOS). Covers frequency band and protocol, addressing and IDs, teach-in, security, acknowledgements, timing, and the drive's control logic.
summary:
I read three Blum patent families in full text, plus single drive-logic patents. A patent shows what Blum describes or claims, not what a given product does. Every protocol finding below needs checking against the owner's actual hardware.

(1) The 2008/2009 family describes radio triggering of SERVO-DRIVE drives, including an AVENTOS flap drive with a plug-in radio module: AT11754U1, DE202009010203U1, ITMI20090269U1, DE202009009963U1 and AT507281B1, priority AT A1345/1346/2008 of 2008-08-29, inventor Taimler. Each battery-powered switch sends a unique ID plus a function code ('ID + Information senden'). The drive-side verification module keeps a list of authorised IDs and ignores unknown ones ('Abbruch'). A switch is taught in by pressing a 'connect' key on the drive, then pressing the switch ('ID = S11 / Funktion = Taste'). A slide switch selects drive-to-drive learning modes ('SYNCHRO', 'CORNER'). An earlier scheme that assigned one radio channel per drive group was dropped because it did not scale. The block diagram labels the radio chip 'nRF' in both the switch and the drive module, and the drive processor 'µC NEC 500 Series'.

(2) The 2009 family (AT508138B1, AU2010268732B2 / WO2011000007) puts the drive's radio interface on its own circuit board, linked to the mainboard by SPI plus digital I/O, with operating buttons on that board. The stated reason is to avoid re-certifying radio approval when either part changes.

(3) The 2020-06-05 family (Ruedisser, Burtscher, Taimler) covers six applications, three already granted in the US: US12698670B2, US12499751B2, US12276150B2, plus AT523880B1, AT523888B1, WO2021243390/392/393/395, the EP4162xxx A1s and US20230236580A1/US20230165384A1. These name ShockBurst / Enhanced ShockBurst (ESB, Nordic Semiconductor's proprietary 2.4 GHz protocol) in the 2.4 GHz ISM band for factory transmitters such as the radio switch. Bluetooth and Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) are for phones, appliances and a WLAN 'bridge' (main transmitter).
- Link behaviour: the control command may be one-way, sent straight to the drive receiver's stored address, with no per-message pairing, no receipt confirmation and no readiness check. The drive receiver is 'in principle in a ready-to-receive state'.
- Timing and routing: drives can forward commands along a fixed route. Actuation is claimed within 100 ms (preferably 50 ms).
- Modes: there is a configuration mode in which addresses and function allocations are stored.
- Security: some embodiments say the radio-switch-to-drive link is 'encrypted and takes place during defined time windows', and mention authentication or signing.
- Commands and state: newer drives may take separate open/close/lock commands, check feasibility, and report status.

(4) Drive logic (US8692497B2, US8066341B2, AT11904U1):
- The drive does a reference run and stops at end positions when arm speed falls below a threshold. It monitors collisions (speed/acceleration against the learned profile) and switches off slightly before the end stop.
- The flap can also be opened or closed by pushing or pulling it (touch function), and a free-wheel coupling allows moving it by hand.
- The same switch closes the flap when it is open. The trigger is therefore a toggle that the drive reads against its current position.

No patent discloses a bit-level frame format, RF channel numbers, data rate, ID or address length, CRC, rolling code or encryption algorithm. None mentions part numbers 23P5020/21P5020. None describes automatic timed closing.

Design consequence: start the 5-minute timer from a flap-position sensor rather than from radio reception. Close by electrically pressing a genuine Blum switch that has been paired normally, ideally a second switch kept for the ESP32. Check with the sensor that the flap closed. Building Blum-compatible radio frames directly is not supported by any published specification, and the encryption embodiments mean it should not be relied on.

findings.claim: Blum's 2020 patent family names (Enhanced) ShockBurst in the 2.4 GHz ISM band as the protocol for control commands from factory transmitters (radio switch, bridge) to the furniture drive. Bluetooth and IEEE 802.11 are named for phones, appliances and the WLAN side. The radio switch is described as opening or closing the flap via ESB.
findings.evidence:
US12698670B2 (Wireless reception and transmission; Ruedisser, Burtscher, Taimler; prio AT A50491/2020, 2020-06-05; PCT/AT2021/060196 = WO2021243395; granted 2026-08-04), col. 4: 'ShockBurst(TM) or Enhanced ShockBurst(TM) are known radio transmission protocols and are designed for operation in the worldwide ISM frequency band at 2.4 GHz. A transmission protocol chosen in such a way can make a minimal energy consumption and minimal latencies for the actuation of at least one furniture element possible.' Col. 5: 'A formation of an input device similar to a remote control—for example in the form of a radio switch—or an operating panel is not to be ruled out.'

US12499751B2 (prio AT A50488/2020; PCT/AT2021/060193; granted 2025-12-16), col. 2: 'ESB (Enhanced ShockBurst) is preferably used as first transmission protocol... ESB makes the transmission of data with a short latency time possible' and 'The combined use of two transmission protocols (ESB and Bluetooth) makes possible the advantage of short latency times for transmitters provided at the factory, through the use of ESB, and at the same time high flexibility in the use of additional devices of any desired make... through the use of Bluetooth.' Col. 6: 'FIGS. 4a and 4b disclose an embodiment example of a physically actuatable switch 5, which transmits signals 4 to the furniture drive 11 via a radio communication. The signals 4 can prompt the furniture drive 11 to open or close the flap 92.' Col. 8: 'Further, the flap 92 can be opened and closed with a switch 5 via ESB.'

US20230165384A1 [0030]: 'The technical term ESB as a radio protocol refers to Enhanced Shockburst(TM), which has proven to be particularly advantageous for controlling furniture drives compared to BLE due to its lower latency periods'.

WO2021243390A1 p.11 (German): 'im Versand-Verfahrensschritt ein Versand gemäß einem dritten ... Übertragungsprotokoll nach ShockBurst(TM) oder nach Enhanced ShockBurst(TM) Standard erfolgen.' KR20230014771A claim 4 also lists ShockBurst/Enhanced ShockBurst (23).
findings.design_impact:
This points to a Nordic-style proprietary 2.4 GHz link, not Wi-Fi or BLE. That fits the 2404-2452 MHz range seen in the FCC filings (cross-link: FCC angle).

My inference, to be confirmed by the hardware angle: the ESP32's own Wi-Fi/BLE radio is not built for ESB. Any direct radio integration would need a Nordic-compatible transceiver plus knowledge of Blum's frame format and security layer, and no patent discloses either.

Recommendation: do not base the BOM on a radio module. Base it on an ESP32 that electrically presses a genuine, paired Blum switch, plus a flap-position sensor. Caveat: the patents date from 2020. Whether the owner's 23P5020 and drive generation actually use ESB is not proven here.

findings.claim: The 2008 Blum radio-trigger family (AVENTOS flap drive with a plug-in radio and verification module) shows a block diagram with radio chips labelled 'nRF' in both the battery-powered switch and the drive-side module. The drive mainboard is labelled 'µC NEC 500 Series' with Flash and 'BUS / DI-DO'. Fig. 2a shows the AVENTOS drive with a detachable module and two switch types: a cylindrical push switch and a framed rocker switch.
findings.evidence:
I read the drawing labels myself from DE202009010203U1, drawing p.7/19, Fig. 1:
- switch S: boxes 'EEPROM', 'µC', 'nRF', 'BATTERIE';
- verification device 1: 'EEPROM' (2), 'µC', 'nRF' (interface 4);
- drive A11: 'Flash', 'µC NEC 500 Series', 'BUS / DI-DO'.
The arrow runs from the switch to the drive module. AT11754U1 page 1 (GM 8053/2009, Anmeldetag 29.08.2008, published 2011-04-15, 'Umwandlung von A 1345/2008', 'MÖBELANORDNUNG MIT DRAHTLOSEM NETZWERK') reproduces the same Fig. 1.

DE202009010203U1 [0030]: 'Der Auslöseschalter S ist natürlich ebenfalls mit einer Schnittstelle zur drahtlosen Kommunikation versehen. Daneben sind noch Komponenten ... wie eine elektronische Speichereinheit, ein Mikrokontroller und eine Batterie, vorgesehen.' [0032]: 'Beispiele für geeignete Schnittstellen zur drahtlosen Kommunikation sind Funkboards.' Fig. 2a: drive A11, removable module 1, two switches S.

That 'nRF' means Nordic Semiconductor is my inference from the label.
findings.design_impact:
This supports a Nordic radio lineage at Blum from about 2008 to 2020. If the owner's switch is the 21P5020-era design (cross-link: FCC/teardown angle), the switch is probably a microcontroller with EEPROM-stored ID, an nRF-type transceiver and a battery.

The daumemo approach (feed 3.3 V in place of the battery and drive the button pads) fits this architecture: the microcontroller wakes on the button press and sends its stored ID.

BOM: a 3.3 V supply and one open-drain GPIO or optocoupler per switch button, not an RF module.

findings.claim: In the 2008 design each trigger switch has a unique identification number, sent with or as the trigger signal (ID + function/information). The drive-side verification device keeps a list of authorised switch IDs, and unknown IDs are ignored. Teach-in: press a 'connect' key on the drive (learning mode), then press the switch, which sends its ID; the list entry is created automatically. A slide switch selects 'SYNCHRO' or 'CORNER' learning modes, and a long press of 'connect' on a second drive sends that drive's ID plus function. A previous scheme assigned one frequency/channel per drive group and was rejected.
findings.evidence:
DE202009010203U1 (Julius Blum GmbH; Unionspriorität AT 1345/2008, 29.08.2008; filed 28.07.2009; registered 29.10.2009; Int Cl H04Q 9/00):
- [0004] '...dass die einem bestimmten Möbelantrieb zugeordneten Auslöseschalter über eine bestimmte Frequenz mit diesem Möbelantrieb kommunizieren, während einem anderen Möbelantrieb zugeordnete Auslöseschalter über eine andere Frequenz ... Über die jeweiligen Frequenzen (Kanäle) kann daher eine Zuordnung ... getroffen werden.' [0005] calls this cumbersome and workable only for small numbers.
- [0008] '...dass alle Auslöseschalter mit einer eindeutigen Identifikationsnummer oder dergleichen versehen sind, welche beispielsweise gemeinsam mit einem oder als Auslösesignal über das drahtlose Netzwerk (zum Beispiel Funknetzwerk, WLAN, IR-Netzwerk) an die Verifikationseinrichtung übermittelt werden kann.'
- [0037] '...sendet dieser ein entsprechendes Signal, welches (auch) seine Identität kodiert ... Die im Signal enthaltene Identifikation wird mit den im elektronischen Speicher 2 abgelegten Datensätzen 3 verglichen.'
- [0038] 'Findet sich die Identifikation allerdings nicht in der Liste, so nimmt die Verifikationseinrichtung 1 keinerlei Aktion vor und es kommt zu einem Abbruch'.

Dies bewirkt, dass dieser Möbelantrieb A21 über seine Schnittstelle seine Identifikation und seine Funktion aussendet.'

DE202009009963U1 [0028]: '...dass jeder Möbelantrieb ... mit seinen Auslöseschaltern ... auf einen bestimmten Funkkanal kommuniziert. Dieses System weist allerdings große Probleme auf, wenn eine bestimmte Anzahl ... überschritten wird.'
findings.design_impact:
The drive is designed to accept several authorised switches. The cleanest integration is therefore to buy a second genuine radio switch, pair it with Blum's normal teach-in procedure (check the manual), and wire the ESP32 to that second switch's button. The owner's handheld switch stays unmodified and keeps working in parallel.

A transmitter that is not taught in will be ignored. No patent discloses the ID or function encoding, so a self-made radio sender has no documented basis.

Whether the owner's drive has a 'connect'/pairing key or slide switch is a question for the owner. The SYNCHRO/CORNER logic means two-drive flaps synchronise drive-to-drive, so triggering one switch is enough.

findings.claim: The 2020 family describes the link to the drive as follows. It can be one-way; it is addressed directly to the drive receiver, so no pairing is needed before each transmission; the receiver address is stored in the control device during a configuration mode. It runs without receipt confirmation, to avoid switching the drive between ready-to-receive and ready-to-transmit modes, and without a readiness check, because the receiver is 'in principle' always ready to receive. Routing can be fixed, with forwarding between drives. Actuation happens within 100 ms (preferably 50 ms) of transmission. Elsewhere bidirectional links and position feedback are 'preferably' provided.
findings.evidence:
US12698670B2, col. 3, transmission measures:
- 'A transmission can be effected unidirectionally between the control device and a receiving device of the at least one furniture element. A bidirectional communication is not to be ruled out...'
- 'A transmission can be effected addressed directly to a receiving device of the at least one furniture element. As a result, a "pairing" being effected before each transmission can be dispensed with, which can have a positive effect on the latencies. The address of the receiving device of a furniture element can have been stored for example in a memory of the control device in a configuration operating mode.'
- 'A transmission can be effected by a transmitting device of the furniture element without a confirmation of receipt. It can thereby be avoided ... that the furniture element has to be toggled between an operating mode in which the furniture element is in a ready-to-receive state and an operating mode in which the furniture element is in a ready-to-transmit state.'
- 'A transmission can be effected without checking the readiness to receive ... the receiving device of the at least one furniture element is in principle in a ready-to-receive state'.
- '...with a fixedly predefined or predefinable routing'.

US12698670B2, col. 6: '...within a period of less than 100 ms, preferably less than 50 ms, from the transmission of the digital control command.' Claim 1 recites under 100 ms; claim 13 under 50 ms. Col. 4-5: user operating mode and configuration operating mode, in which 'addresses of the receiving device of the furniture elements, function allocations ... can be stored'.

US12499751B2, col. 2: 'At least one transmission protocol, preferably all transmission protocols, are preferably bidirectional. Thereby, it is in particular possible to receive feedback of the furniture elements, in particular feedback of their current position.'

The same one-way/direct-address/no-ACK wording appears in AT523880B1 (granted 2024-09-15, 'Zweikanal-Empfang', A 50492/2020) and in WO2021243390A1 p.11-12: '...kann ein vor jedem Versand erfolgendes Koppeln ("pairing") entfallen...'.
findings.design_impact:
The mains-powered drive is described as always listening. A press on a paired switch is therefore not bound to any wake window on the drive side; the button-timing constraints come from the switch, see daumemo (0.8 s press).

The link may have no ACK, so neither the switch nor the ESP32 can know from the radio side that a command arrived. The firmware must close the loop with its own sensor: a reed or hall sensor on the flap, optionally an accelerometer. It should expect motion to start within about 100 ms to 1 s, then confirm the end state.

With fixed routing and drive-to-drive forwarding, one command per flap is enough, even with two drive units.

findings.claim: Blum's 2020 applications describe embodiments in which the radio-switch-to-drive link (and the app/setup link) is encrypted and enabled only in defined time windows. Authentication or signing is mentioned as preferable. They also describe separate fitter and end-user configuration areas.
findings.evidence:
US20230236580A1 (Method for operating an assembly; prio 2020-06-05; = AT523887A1 / CN116134204A):
- [0125] 'FIG. 2c differs from FIG. 2a in so far as the command transmitter 7 is present in the form of a radio switch element 16. A data communication between the data forwarding device 8 of the command transmitter 7 and the data forwarding device 8 of the furniture drive 2 is encrypted and takes place during defined time windows.'
- [0071] '...a data communication between the at least one data forwarding device of the at least one command transmitter and the at least one data forwarding device of the at least one furniture drive is enabled in encrypted form and/or during defined time windows.'
- [0072] '...it is particularly preferable to provide an authentication and/or signing of data and/or an encryption of a data link.'
- Claim 17 has the same wording.

US20230165384A1 [0025]: '...the assembly operator area and the end user region are separated from each other, preferably by separate logins and/or separate apps ... data communication between the at least one electronic device and the at least one furniture drive is enabled in encrypted form and/or during defined time windows.' EP4162136A1 (Google Patents snippet) has the same wording.

These are optional embodiments, not proof of what the 23P5020 implements.
findings.design_impact:
A design that re-creates Blum radio frames cannot be assumed to work; encryption or freshness checks may be implemented. I did not research this further. It strengthens the case for the hardware path: electrically actuate a genuine, paired switch.

To detect the OPEN event, use a flap sensor rather than radio. This also catches openings by the touch function or by other switches.

The word 'bidirectional' on Blum's 23P5020 documents fits the bidirectional/feedback language here (cross-link: Blum docs/FCC angle).

findings.claim: Blum's granted architecture has a 'main transmitter' (central bridge to WLAN/cloud/voice/app) and 'auxiliary transmitters' (a physical switch, an appliance, or a transmitter in another furniture element), all controlling the same drive receiver. The receiver can take both transmitters' signals at the same time. Movement can be blocked based on another element's position, for example a lock or a collision-prone neighbour. An app configures both transmitters with the drive.
findings.evidence:
US12276150B2 (Device for controlling at least one electrically drivable or movable furniture element; prio AT A50493/2020; PCT/AT2021/060195; granted 2025-04-15):
- Abstract: 'A device for controlling a movable furniture element includes a main transmitter, an auxiliary transmitter, and a receiver. The auxiliary transmitter is separate from the main transmitter.'
- Col. 3: 'This main transmitter can therefore function as an interface ("bridge") between the wireless network and the furniture drives.'
- Col. 8: 'In addition, a program ("app") for configuring the furniture elements 1 can be present, by means of which both the main transmitter 31 and the auxiliary transmitter 32 can be configured with the associated furniture element 1 ... the movement of a furniture element 1 can be prohibited on the basis of the position and/or movement of another furniture element 1'.
- Claim 1(i): '...the first receiver is configured to receive the first wireless signal and the second wireless signal simultaneously'.
- Col. 4 repeats the ESB wording: 'unidirectionally ... addressed directly ... without an acknowledgement of receipt ... wherein ESB (Enhanced ShockBurst) is preferably used'.
findings.design_impact:
The planned ESP32 device is functionally Blum's 'main transmitter'. Blum's own design lets several transmitters drive one receiver, which supports adding a dedicated second paired switch under ESP32 control.

If the owner's drive generation is supported by a Blum bridge or app product, that could be an official route to timed closing (cross-link: product/app angle; not verified here).

findings.claim: Newer drives may combine ESB and Bluetooth receivers, sharing one antenna by alternating between them under time scheduling. They can exchange status or position for collision avoidance and synchronisation, accept explicit open, close, lock and unlock commands, check feasibility as a Boolean, and return status such as 'cupboard has been opened'. An appliance can send a locking command to prevent an unwanted close.
findings.evidence:
US12499751B2, col. 7: '...when both signals 401, 402 are transmitted on different carrier frequencies, such that two antennas are necessary for receiving the radio signals. But two receiving units 21, 22 can also share an antenna, wherein in this case typically signals 401, 402 are received via the first or the second transmission protocol alternately. The time scheduling for reception and sending time must, for instance, be executed by a program, which runs in the receiver 2 and in transmitters 3'. Col. 4: status data 'describe the position and/or movement status of at least one furniture drive ... for avoiding collisions and/or for synchronising'.

US20230236580A1:
- [0121] 'The digital command 9 can comprise in the form of a closing command or an opening command ... and/or a locking command or an unlocking command'.
- [0122] 'The selection is transferred to a Boolean variable'.
- [0132] 'A status message such as "cupboard has been opened" can be displayed'.
- [0089] '...the household appliance can also automatically transmit a locking command to the furniture drive ... in order to inhibit an unwanted closing for safety reasons.'
- [0111] 'The command transmitters 7 communicate with the data forwarding devices 8 of the furniture drives 2 via ESB, wherein the smartphone can additionally communicate directly ... via ELB' (sic).
findings.design_impact:
On newer generations a Bluetooth/app interface may exist and could be a supported integration path; ask the owner. A shared antenna means the ESB listening may not be continuous, so a genuine switch press is the safest trigger.

There is a conflict to note: the 2020 architecture has explicit open/close commands, while the 2005-2007 patents describe one toggle trigger. The firmware must not assume which one the owner's switch sends, so verify the flap state before and after each actuation.

findings.claim: Blum's control concept for flap drives is a single trigger that the drive interprets by its current position: the same switch opens and closes. The flap can also be opened or closed by pulling or pushing it (touch function), and a free-wheel coupling allows moving it by hand. Battery-free radio switches using piezo or electrodynamic energy are described as an option.
findings.evidence:
US8066341B2 (Item of furniture; Brüstle; prio AT A478/2005, 2005-03-21; granted 2011-11-29):
- 'The switch device can also activate the electric drive by wireless transmission means.'
- '...the electric drive can be activated by pulling or pushing the flap. These types of functions are known as touch latch functions, where the flap can be moved into the fully open as well as the fully closed position by being pulled or pushed.'
- 'An activation device 35 assesses the signals of devices 30-34 ... to a control and regulating device 36 which in turn can control electric drive 5 and also flap 2 in accordance with a selectable operating mode.'
- Claims cover a coupling with free wheel.

AT11904U1 (GM 8087/2010; Anmeldetag 24.05.2007; from A 824/2007; published 2011-07-15):
- [0009] '...kann das Schließen der Klappe ... ganz einfach dadurch erfolgen, dass der Benutzer das nun nicht mehr durch das Möbelteil verdeckte Schaltelement unmittelbar betätigt.'
- [0018] 'Das Schaltelement kann auch als Funkschalter realisiert werden. Insbesondere ist es möglich, derartige Funkschalter ohne Batterien auszubilden, wobei die für den Funkbetrieb benötigte Stromerzeugung mittels eines Piezokristalls oder elektrodynamisch (zum Beispiel durch eine Tauchspule) erfolgt.'

DE202005021123U1 (prio AT A1378/2004): [0009] Funksender / Funkempfänger; [0011] 'Piezokristall ... piezoelektrische Energie zur Versorgung des Funksenders'.
findings.design_impact:
This supports daumemo's toggle finding. Consequences:
- A flap-state sensor (reed + magnet or hall) is mandatory.
- Start the 5-minute timer on the sensed transition to 'open', whether triggered by switch, touch or manual movement.
- Before sending the closing press, check the flap is still open. Otherwise a late press would re-open a flap someone already closed.
- Cancel the timer if the flap closes early.
- Sensor BOM: one reed or hall sensor, magnet, and a pull-up on an ESP32 GPIO.

findings.claim: Blum drive electronics: the radio interface sits on a separate board from the drive mainboard, inside the same housing (flap actuating drive embodiment). It links to the mainboard through a board-to-board contact using SPI plus digital I/O, is powered through the mainboard, and has operating buttons on the radio board. The stated reason is to avoid re-certification under national radio rules. A related drive patent offers the same drive with either a cable-interface board or a radio board, and links two drives of one part with a synchronisation cable.

findings.design_impact:
Older drive generations may have a swappable radio or cable module, with the pairing button probably on the radio board. Some Blum drives used wired switches through a cable board.

If the owner's drive has a wired switch input or cable-switch accessory, the ESP32 could trigger it through a potential-free contact (relay or optocoupler) with no radio at all. That would be the simplest and most robust option; ask the owner.

Warning: do not tap the drive's internal SPI or mainboard. It is undocumented, and doing so risks damage and safety problems.

findings.claim: Drive-to-drive coordination includes timer-based inhibition, where one drive blocks another for a set time after triggering in corner setups. Before moving, a drive queries the other drive's closed position over radio, so the drive modules also transmit. A 2010 Blum 'securing apparatus' prevents simultaneous opening of collision-prone parts and can use radio.
findings.evidence:
DE202009010203U1:
- [0043] '...dass für eine bestimmte Zeit nach erfolgtem Auslösen eines der beiden Möbelantriebe A11 oder A21 ... es auch zu einem Auslösen des anderen Möbelantriebs ... kommt ... Die entsprechende Zeitdauer kann durch einen Timer festgelegt werden.'
- [0044] '...fragt die Verifikationseinrichtung 1 des ersten Möbelantriebs A11 bei der Verifikationseinrichtung 1 des zweiten Möbelantriebs A21 nach, in welcher Schließlage sich das bewegbare Möbelteil ... befindet.'
- Fig. 5b: 'Abfrage Antrieb A12 -> Front geschlossen: Bewegung A11 auslösen / Front geöffnet: Abbruch'.

findings.design_impact:
In multi-flap or corner cabinets the drive may refuse a command because of interlocks. Firmware should treat 'no movement after press' as a normal outcome and report it, not retry endlessly.

The drive modules have transmitters as well as receivers, which fits Blum's 'bidirectional' wording on the 23P5020.

negative_results: Google Patents query endpoint, assignee 'Julius Blum', q = wireless, radio, transmitter, receiver, remote control, bluetooth, pairing, teach-in, learning mode, identifier, identification code, encryption, rolling code, frequency, acknowledgement, bidirectional, radio switch, radio module, energy saving mode, sleep mode, wake (21 queries, 784 unique hits). No Blum document discloses a bit-level frame format, RF channel numbers, data rate, address/ID length, CRC, rolling-code counter or encryption algorithm. 'Rolling code' hits were all mechanical. 'Encryption' hits were only the 2020-06-05 family (CN116134204A, EP4162136A1).
No Blum patent I read names part numbers 23P5020/21P5020 or links to FCC IDs W95-*; patents do not normally do this. Matching patents to products is left to the FCC and manuals angles.

No Blum patent I read describes automatic timed closing of a flap after a delay. The closest are a timer that blocks a second drive after triggering (DE202009010203U1 [0043]) and user-defined times when a part may not be opened (US20230165384A1 [0013], US20230236580A1 [0075]). An adjustable auto-close period appears only in a competitor patent, EP2717105A2 (Grass GmbH, ZigBee/Z-Wave), not Blum.

Refuted leads: US6832072B2 'Wireless switch' is Inncom International (hotel IR/RF energy management), not Blum. EP1323363A1 (Blum, 2001) has no radio content; it covers force-sensor servo assist only.
AT18049U1 (2020, hydraulic transmission flap drive) and DE212020000657U1 (2019, door drive) mention a radio switch or radio module only as an option, with no protocol, pairing or security details.

No Blum patent found on wake-up or duty-cycling of the drive receiver. The 2020 family states the receiver is 'in principle in a ready-to-receive state'; the switch's sleep behaviour is not described.

No channel-hopping scheme found. The 2008 family mentions per-group fixed channels only as rejected prior art; the 2020 family mentions different carrier frequencies for ESB and Bluetooth and alternating reception on a shared antenna.

Access limits; nothing was circumvented:
- Justia, FreePatentsOnline, uspto.report and WIPO Patentscope returned HTTP 403.
- Google Patents HTML pages returned 503, and the query endpoint began returning 'unusual traffic' pages after about 21 queries, so I stopped using it.
- The DEPATISnet full PDF needs a captcha (not bypassed); only DEPATISnet bibliographic data was used.
- Espacenet was not used (JavaScript-only).
- The session's web-search budget ran out. As a result, German-term searches (Anlernen, Kennung, Rollcode, Zeitfenster) and a check of WO2017177247A1 (cited in US12499751B2 as the flap drive of its Fig. 1) were not done.
open_questions: Which patent generation matches the owner's hardware? Either the 2008-era design (drive radio module with 'connect' key, switch ID list) or the 2020-era ESB/Bluetooth design (encryption/time-window embodiments, explicit open/close commands). Check against the FCC exhibits and manuals.
Does the 23P5020/21P5020 send one toggle trigger or separate OPEN/CLOSE commands? The 2005-2007 patents imply toggle; the 2020 patents describe explicit commands.
Is encryption or freshness protection actually implemented on the 23P5020-to-drive link? The patents describe it only as an option.
Does the owner's drive offer a wired switch input (Blum 'Kabelboard' / cable switch accessory), which would allow a potential-free contact trigger with no radio?
Is there an official Blum bridge, hub or app (the 'main transmitter' of US12276150B2) for the owner's drive generation? That could provide supported scheduling or automation.

Content of WO2017177247A1, which US12499751B2 cites as the flap drive of its Fig. 1a/1b, and the remaining WO numbers of the 2020 family (for example the PCT/AT2021/060195 publication) were not verified.

Legal status was taken only from document fronts. The EP4162136A1/EP4162461A1/EP4162648A1 applications were not checked in a register. The 2007-2009 AT/DE utility models are probably expired (10-year maximum term; inference).
questions_for_user: What part numbers are printed on the drive unit(s) and on the radio switch (for example 23P5020 vs 21P5020)? Photos of both labels, the drive's visible buttons or slide switches, and any sockets would help.
Which AVENTOS type is it (HF / HS / HL / HK), and does the flap have one drive unit or two linked by a cable?
Does the drive have a visible pairing / 'connect' / reset button, a slide switch, or a socket for a wired switch?
Does your system use any Blum app, Bluetooth pairing, or Blum hub/bridge, or only the radio switch?
Would you buy a second Blum radio switch, pair it normally, and dedicate it to the ESP32 (opening it to wire the button), so your handheld switch stays unmodified?
Can a magnet and reed or hall sensor be mounted on the flap and carcass to detect open/closed?
Do children or pets use the cabinet? Is an automatic close acceptable with a warning beep or light, and is a presence sensor wanted?
What power is available near the cabinet: Blum 24 V supply, USB, or mains outlet? Which region are you in (EU/US)?
